planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed.

directions: An old Southern Cone Cucurbita maxima landrace whose ribbed, blue-gray fruit (the name translates roughly to 'lead-colored squash') hides deep orange, notably dry and dense flesh prized for soups and the classic Argentine stew locro. Vines sprawl widely and tolerate squash bug pressure better than many maxima types, so give them room and steady moisture through fruit set rather than crowding them against other cucurbits. Harvest once the rind resists a thumbnail and the stem has corked over, then cure fruit in a warm, airy spot for a couple of weeks to firm up the flesh and extend winter storage. Its long storage life made it a reliable staple squash for Andean-foothill households well before refrigeration.

planting.note: Plant seed tubers once soil is workable; hill as foliage grows.

directions: One of the hundreds of native potato landraces still grown on Chile's Chiloé Archipelago, a globally recognized center of potato diversity, with a dark purple-black skin and a floury, deeply flavored flesh notable for frying well without excessive oil absorption. Chilote growers have maintained michuñe and its many sister varieties for generations in small mixed plots using traditional rotation and seed-saving practices suited to the archipelago's cool, wet climate. Plant whole or cut seed tubers in loose, humus-rich soil, hill soil around stems as they emerge, and keep moisture even but not waterlogged since the maritime-climate landrace resents both drought and soggy ground. Harvest after the vines die back and cure tubers briefly in a dark, cool spot before storage.
sources: Universidad Austral de Chile potato germplasm studies
Slow Food Foundation Ark of Taste — Chiloé potato documentation

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines or rooted cuttings in early spring.

directions: Brought to Chile from Spain in the 16th century as one of the first Vitis vinifera varieties planted in the Americas, País (known as Criolla Chica in Argentina and Mission grape in California) is a hardy, drought-tolerant red long cultivated on own-rooted, unirrigated head-trained vines in central and southern Chile. Many surviving plantings are over a century old and were historically used for everyday table wine and the lightly sparkling pipeño style rather than premium bottling. Grow on own roots in lean, well-drained soil with minimal irrigation once established, since the variety is adapted to dry-farmed conditions and overwatering dilutes its naturally light color and body. Prune to an old-fashioned head or goblet form for best air circulation in humid years, and expect generous yields of loose clusters that ripen into a fresh, easy-drinking red.
sources: South America Wine Guide — País, Pipeño & Criolla

common_name: Torrontés Riojano Grape (Argentine Heritage White Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines or rooted cuttings in early spring.

directions: A natural cross of Muscat of Alexandria and the colonial-era Criolla Chica grape, Torrontés Riojano is the aromatic white considered uniquely Argentina's own, reaching its finest, most floral expression in the high-altitude vineyards around Cafayate, Salta. Clusters produce intensely perfumed, rose- and jasmine-scented fruit that is usually vinified dry despite its sweet-smelling aroma. The vine performs best with the big diurnal temperature swings of high-elevation desert sites, where warm days build sugar and cool nights preserve the grape's signature aromatics and acidity. Train on a sturdy trellis in full sun with minimal irrigation, and prune to open the canopy for airflow since humid, low-altitude sites blunt both its aroma and disease resistance.

A traditional Andean flour corn grown for centuries by Quechua and Aymara communities in Argentina's northwestern Calchaquí Valley provinces of Catamarca, Salta, and Jujuy, prized for its large, plump, ivory-white to pale-pink kernels with an exceptionally soft, floury interior. Its defining use is capia, a regional pastry batter made by mixing the ground flour with egg yolk, sugar, and rendered fat, then filled with dulce de leche for valley festivals. Plant in blocks rather than single rows to ensure good pollination, and give the tall stalks rich soil and consistent moisture through tasseling and ear fill. Let ears dry fully in the husk before harvest, since the variety's culinary value depends on a thoroughly cured, starchy kernel rather than fresh eating quality.
sources: Slow Food Foundation Ark of Taste — Capia Corn
ResearchGate — maize variety identification in the Hualfín valley, Catamarca

directions: A large-seeded, speckled brown soup pea representative of the traditional Latvian gray pea group recognized by Slow Food's Ark of Taste and protected under EU geographic designation, brought to North American growers by way of a seed exchange with an Irish seed-saver. Vigorous vines reach four to five feet and carry pink-and-red bicolor flowers quite unlike the white blossoms of common green soup peas, making it a distinctive sight on the trellis. In Latvia the dried peas are the heart of a Christmas-season stew simmered whole with diced onion and fatty pork, so let pods mature and dry fully on the vine rather than picking for fresh eating. Provide a tall trellis or brush support and well-drained soil, since the long vines and dense pod set can lodge in exposed, windy gardens.
sources: Slow Food Foundation Ark of Taste — Latvian Big Grey Peas

directions: Bred at Estonia's Jõgeva Plant Breeding Institute by horticulturist Julius Aamisepp, who also developed the long-popular Jõgeva Yellow potato, this early, high-yielding garden pea has remained a fixture of Baltic home gardens for decades thanks to its reliable performance in cool, short-season springs. Semi-tall vines carry slightly curved, well-filled pods holding seven to nine sweet, juicy peas, and plants show notably strong resistance to the damp-weather diseases common in northern climates. Sow as soon as the soil can be worked, since the variety's main advantage is tolerating cold, wet starts that would rot less hardy peas, and provide light twig or netting support to keep the semi-tall vines upright. Harvest frequently at the fresh-shell stage for the sweetest flavor, or let pods mature further for freezing and canning.
sources: Wikipedia — Julius Aamisepp biography and plant breeding career

planting.note: Plant seed tubers once soil is workable; hill as foliage grows.

directions: A smooth-skinned, creamy pink landrace from the Chiloé Archipelago, one of several hundred named native potato varieties still maintained by Chilote smallholders and a key reservoir of the genetic diversity behind today's global potato crop. Its high moisture content and creamy texture after cooking make it a traditional choice for milcao and potato tortilla rather than for frying or baking. Plant seed tubers in loose, fertile soil as soon as it is workable, hilling soil up around stems as they grow to keep developing tubers covered and shaded. Keep moisture steady through tuber bulking in the archipelago's characteristically cool, humid climate, and harvest after vines have died back, curing tubers briefly before storage.
